newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bankers welcome govt Euro cost proposal.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bankers welcome govt Euro cost proposal.

text.p: Belgian bankers gave a cautious welcome to a proposal by Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt which would allow them to provision part of the cost of the introduction of the European single currency in 1999.

"This will allow us to prepare for the cost of the introduction of the Euro while our earnings are still good, while we still benefit from the positive impact of falling interest rates," Banque Bruxelles Lambert chief executive officer Daniel Cardon de Lichtbuer told Reuters at the Belgian Banking Association (BBA) annual meeting.
In a speech to the meeting, Maystadt said he would consider letting banks provision the exceptional costs related to the introduction of the European single currency.

"Considering the size of the exceptional costs the banking sector will incur, I have asked...to investigate to which extent certain costs linked to the Euro could not already be provisioned in financial institutions' balance sheets," he said.
Maystadt comments received applause from the hundreds of bankers present at the meeting.
But he warned only exceptional costs could be provisioned, and not the loss of income from foreign exchange trading that is to be expected when the single currency comes into being.
Late last month the banking association said it wanted the Belgian state to compensate part of the estimated 35 billion franc cost of switching to the Euro.
The association said that converting computer systems to the Euro will cost 15 billion francs, lost income from currency trade 15 billon and the conversion of cash money five billion.

Philippe Cloes, chief executive of Credit Lyonnais Bank Belgium, told Reuters that in a normal, competitive market banks should be able to pay the cost of change and pass on part of that cost to their customers.
"Allowing us to provision part of the cost of the Euro de facto means a delay in taxation, so what we are talking about is the time value of money," he said.
But he added that at current low interest rates, the benefit for the sector was not that great.

If banks were not allowed to provision Euro-related costs now, they would be forced to book them as operating costs in their profit and loss accounts of 1997 and 1998, which would hurt more if profits in these years were hit by other factors.
Provisioning allows bank to smooth out the impact on earnings over a longer period.
Wim Coumans, chief executive officer of industrial credit bank NMKN/SNCI, told Reuters that Maystadt's proposal did not make clear just what could be provisioned.
"If it means that we can provision now costs we will make in the future, that is fine. But does that mean I can provision now part of the future wage costs of the computer department?"
He and others also wondered whether the provisioning could start for the 1996 financial year already. Bankers need to know as they have to make tax prepayments by December 20.
"It is already early December, it seems difficult to get clarity on this issue by the end of the month," BBA director Georges Martin said.
